title: The wrong bishop: a rook pawn that cannot win
outcomes: Predicts win or draw for a rook pawn with a bishop, from the bishop's colour and the pawn's file
Names what can rescue a 'wrong bishop' win: another pawn file, or a defending king that cannot reach the corner
Tests a rook-pawn-and-bishop ending for the three conditions before predicting win or draw

steps.text: A bishop and a **rook pawn** (a- or h-file) do not always win. If the bishop cannot control the pawn's queening corner, a defending king that reaches that corner can draw. The colour of the bishop and the file of the pawn decide. Watch what the same set-up does with a different bishop or a different pawn.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop travels on dark squares; a8 is light. One line is shown.

line.say: Black's king steps next to the corner.
Black's king goes back to the corner.

steps.text: **What decides it:** (1) the bishop's colour against the queening square, (2) the pawn's file, (3) whether Black's king can reach the corner in time. Change any one of them and the result can flip. Predict each look-alike first.

steps.title: Same bishop, other pawn
steps.prompt: The dark-squared bishop with a pawn on the b-file instead. Is it still a draw? Predict, then check.

steps.title: Same pawn, other bishop
steps.prompt: The a-pawn again, with a light-squared bishop. Is it still a draw? Predict, then check.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, and when it fails.** A rook pawn with a bishop that does not control the queening corner is a draw *if* the defending king can get to the corner. It fails when the defending king is cut off from the corner (the last position), when the pawn stands on another file, or when the bishop does control the corner. Check the king's distance before you trust the draw.

steps.prompt: Look back at your predictions. Which condition did you check first: bishop colour, pawn file, or where the black king stood? Name one prediction where skipping a condition would have misled you, then rate how sure you are now.
